cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Ba Xian strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a medium-light oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted medium; a thick leaf that takes roast well and is often given two passes.
harvest_season: Spring, late April into May; a late-sprouting strain with a large leaf, picked once, with autumn lots rare.
appearance_dry: Long, broad, dark brown strips, heavier than most dancong, with a sweet-floral and slightly resinous smell.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, leathery olive leaves with strong red edges.
taste_profile: A high, sharp orchid aroma with honey and a distinct bitter edge up front that turns into a long, sweet, cooling aftertaste; thick body and a mineral, almost savoury finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, very fast pours; this strain is the bitterest of the classic dancongs when over-steeped and the sweetest in the throat when brewed right. A little less leaf than for Mi Lan Xiang helps.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually released in autumn after a medium roast and a few months of rest; its thick leaf and roast make it one of the better-keeping dancongs, good for three to five years sealed and dry and sometimes sold aged with the year stated.
description:
Ba Xian, the Eight Immortals, is the Phoenix dancong with the most bite: a big-leaved, late-sprouting strain whose cup pairs a high orchid-and-honey aroma with a frank bitterness that turns, a few seconds later, into one of the longest sweet aftertastes in the family. It is a drinker's tea rather than a sniffer's tea.

The name comes from a story about its propagation: cuttings were taken from one old tree, eight of them survived and were planted in different gardens, and someone called them the eight immortals crossing the sea. The details, including the name and site of the mother tree, are hard to pin down, so take it as a story. The strain has spread across the Fenghuang range.

The leaf is thick and tolerates a proper medium charcoal roast, so Ba Xian is usually darker in the bag than Ya Shi Xiang or Zhi Lan Xiang and is often roasted twice. The roast knits the bitterness into the honey and gives the tea a density that most dancongs lack. In the cup the aroma is a sharp orchid, the first impression is slightly bitter and mineral, and then the hui gan, the returning sweetness, arrives and stays for minutes.

Brewing is about speed. Use a touch less leaf than for a Mi Lan Xiang, boiling water and genuinely instant pours for the first steeps; a lazy ten seconds gives you bitterness without the sweetness. Done right it runs eight or more infusions and the later ones are pure sugar-cane.

It is sold by year, usually in autumn, and it keeps better than most dancong thanks to the roast, so a lot from last year is not a problem and may be a bonus. The name is distinct from the Zhao'an Ba Xian oolong of southern Fujian, a different cultivar that shares only the immortals. If Ba Xian is too much, Huang Zhi Xiang is a gentler dancong with a gardenia aroma.
sources_note: The Qu Zai Liao mother tree at Li Zai Ping and the eight-cuttings story follow Chaozhou tea sources and are presented as a story.
history:
Ba Xian is a strain of the Fenghuang dancong family from the Chaozhou mountains in Guangdong, and it is placed in the zhi lan, or orchid, aroma group. Its older name is Ba Xian Guo Hai, the Eight Immortals crossing the sea. One Chinese overview describes large, heavy, tightly rolled dark leaf, a bright golden liquor and a strong returning sweetness. It adds that a particular handling or a sudden swing in temperature and humidity during making can tip the aroma towards osmanthus.

The usual story says cuttings from one old tree were planted out, eight of them took, and the name followed. No dated record turned up behind that story, nor a firm account of the mother tree or who propagated it, so the early history of this strain remains thinly documented.
